name: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
authors: Yilun Du, Shuang Li, Antonio Torralba, Joshua B. Tenenbaum (MIT CSAIL), Igor Mordatch (Google Brain); first author Du et al.
venue: ICML 2024 (Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235:11733-11763). First submitted to arXiv May 2023 (arXiv:2305.14325).
reflection_type: multi-agent-debate. Multiple instances of the same LLM independently propose candidate answers, then over several rounds each agent reads and critiques the responses of all other agents (concatenated as context) and revises its own answer until the population converges to a shared final answer. Explicitly framed as a 'society of minds' approach and contrasted with single-instance verbal self-reflection (Reflexion/Self-Refine).
feedback_source: self-generated (the critique signal comes entirely from other instances of the same black-box LLM; no external tool, unit test, environment reward, or ground-truth oracle is used at inference time). Answers are extracted from the agents' own generations; for evaluation only, ground truth is used to score accuracy but not fed back into the debate.
iteration_structure: iterative-refine across multiple parallel agents. Default configuration is 3 agents and 2 rounds of debate; ablations scale the number of agents and the number of rounds (gains plateau beyond ~4 rounds). Each round all agents simultaneously regenerate conditioned on the others' previous-round answers (a fixed-round, no-reset refinement, not retry-with-reset or tree/MCTS search).
reflection_object: output content and the reasoning chain. Each agent reflects on and revises its own answer plus its chain-of-thought reasoning in light of the other agents' full responses (and reasoning). No prompt/context engineering, skill library, rules/constitution, or weight update is modified — only the natural-language answers are iteratively rewritten across rounds.
requires_training: none (training-free, inference-time only; requires only black-box access to LLM generations — no likelihoods, gradients, or fine-tuning). The authors note debate transcripts could later be distilled back into the base model for self-improvement, but this is not done in the paper.
reward_or_critic_model: self-as-judge — each LLM agent acts as both proposer and critic of the other agents' answers. There is no trained reward model, no verifiable reward, and no separate retrospective/meta-judge model; the consensus emerges from peer agents critiquing each other.
distillation_target: none in the paper itself (no reusable artifact is produced; each task is solved fresh at inference). The authors explicitly suggest debate outputs could be distilled to model-weights as a future self-improvement loop, but this is proposed as future work, not implemented.
emergent_vs_engineered: engineered / prompt-scaffold-based. The debate behavior is induced by fixed hand-written prompt templates (a 'consensus prompt' inserting [other answers]) and an orchestration loop over agents and rounds; it is not an RL-emergent reflective behavior. Short vs long debate prompts are used to tune how 'stubborn' agents are and thus convergence speed.
memory_type: short-term/scratchpad — within a single debate, each agent's context window holds the concatenation (or a summarized version) of all other agents' current responses, which serves as transient working memory. No long-term episodic store, skill library, or cross-task playbook is maintained.
memory_persistence: within-episode only. The debate context is rebuilt per query and discarded; nothing persists across tasks or sessions.
memory_curation_mechanism: self-summarized/curated (optional). When many agents participate (5+), instead of directly concatenating all responses the method first summarizes other agents' responses (using the LLM) into a single response per round to fit context limits; this summarization both reduces context length and was found to improve performance. Otherwise the default is append/concatenate of the latest-round responses.
error_localization_granularity: holistic/outcome-level at the level of each agent's whole answer, combined with agent-level cross-examination (each agent critiques the other agents' full responses). The method does not localize errors to specific reasoning steps, code blocks, or tokens; it operates on complete candidate responses that agents accept, reject, or merge.
intra_task_vs_inter_task: intra-task. All reflection/debate happens within the solving of a single query; there is no transfer of learned experience across tasks (unlike Reflexion/ExpeL). The improvement comes from multiple agents reconciling within one problem instance.
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: mid-trajectory-recovery (in-flight, within the debate). The paper highlights cases where all agents initially produce wrong answers but converge to the correct answer over debate rounds, i.e. errors are corrected mid-process rather than only avoided on a later retry. There is no cross-episode retry/reset.
task_domains: math (arithmetic, grade-school word problems), QA/reasoning (MMLU factual multiple-choice), strategic reasoning / decision-making (chess next-move prediction), and factuality/hallucination (biography generation). Broadly: reasoning, factuality, and question-answering.
benchmarks: Arithmetic (custom 6-operand two-digit expressions, 100 problems), GSM8K (grade-school math, 100 problems), Chess Move Prediction (300 grandmaster games, Stockfish pawn-score), a newly introduced Biographies benchmark (524 well-known computer scientists, ground-truth bullet facts from Wikipedia), MMLU (100 questions), and Chess Move Validity (BIG-Bench Chess-State Tracking, synthetic_short hardest split, 100 tasks).
headline_result: With gpt-3.5-turbo (chatGPT), 3 agents x 2 rounds of debate vs single-agent baseline: Arithmetic 67.0% -> 81.8%, GSM8K 77.0% -> 85.0%, Chess pawn-score 91.4 -> 122.9 (reasoning, Table 1); Biographies 66.0% -> 73.8%, MMLU 63.9% -> 71.1%, Chess Move Validity 29.3% -> 45.2% (factuality, Table 2). Debate is the best method on every task.
baselines: (1) Single Agent (zero-shot CoT direct generation); (2) Single Agent (Reflection) — the model self-critiques its own first generation (Reflexion/Self-Refine style); (3) Multi-Agent (Majority) — multiple agents generate and answers are combined by majority voting (omitted on factuality tasks where responses are not directly comparable). All baselines use identical starting prompts and the same LLM (gpt-3.5-turbo-0301).
gains_vs_baseline: Debate beats the strongest baseline on each task. Reasoning (vs best of single-reflection / majority): Arithmetic 81.8 vs 72.1 (reflection) ~ +9.7 pts; GSM8K 85.0 vs 81.0 (majority) ~ +4.0 pts; Chess 122.9 vs 102.2 (majority) ~ +20.7 pawn-score. Factuality (vs reflection): Biographies 73.8 vs 68.3 ~ +5.5 pts; MMLU 71.1 vs 57.7 ~ +13.4 pts (notably, reflection HURT MMLU, dropping 63.9 -> 57.7); Chess Validity 45.2 vs 38.8 ~ +6.4 pts. Both multiple agents AND multiple rounds are needed for best results; using different persona-initialization prompts raised MMLU further from 71.1 to 74.2.
compute_cost_profile: Substantially higher inference cost than a single forward pass: roughly N_agents x N_rounds LLM generations (default 3 agents x 2 rounds ~ 6x, growing with more agents/rounds), plus growing context length as responses are concatenated each round. The paper acknowledges this is 'more computationally expensive' and uses response summarization to bound context for >=5 agents. No training cost (inference-only method).
known_limitations: (1) Higher computational/API cost (multiple generations and rounds). (2) As debates lengthen, current LLMs struggle to process the full debate context and tend to focus only on the most recent generations (mitigable with longer-context models or summarization). (3) Convergence is to a consensus that is NOT guaranteed correct — agents sometimes converge confidently on a wrong answer and affirm it as correct/consistent, attributed to poorly expressed model uncertainty. (4) On confidently-held (often wrong) facts, agents are hard to persuade to change. (5) Convergence is empirical, not theoretically guaranteed (debate is a multi-agent game).
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: intrinsic-only / self-verify. The debate uses no external tool, verifier, or ground-truth label as feedback — improvement arises purely from multiple instances of the same LLM cross-examining each other. This makes it a notable case where multi-agent self-critique yields net gains without oracle feedback (distinguishing it from single-agent self-reflection, which the paper shows can degrade performance, e.g. MMLU 63.9 -> 57.7 under Reflection).
self_correction_efficacy: net-positive across all six tasks under the multi-agent debate setup (improves over single-agent and over single-agent reflection on every benchmark, with no ground-truth feedback). This contrasts with the paper's own single-agent Reflection baseline, which is task-dependent and net-negative on MMLU. The mechanism (diversity across multiple instances + peer critique) is what makes self-correction work here, since errors that are not shared across agents tend to be filtered out.
calibration_effect: mixed / partially improves. Debate reduces hallucinated and internally-uncertain facts because agents disagree on uncertain facts and omit them, improving factual reliability. However, the paper explicitly notes residual overconfidence: agents confidently affirm converged answers even when wrong, and direct confidence elicitation gives uniformly high confidence — i.e. calibration of the final consensus is imperfect. Calibration is discussed qualitatively, not measured with a formal calibration metric.
failure_attribution_capability: n/a — this is a method paper for improving reasoning/factuality, not a failure-attribution or failure-taxonomy study. It does not classify failure modes, attribute a responsible agent, or localize a failing step in a structured way.
failure_mode_addressed: Targets hallucination / fabricated facts (notably in biography generation and MMLU) and reasoning errors / implausible reasoning jumps in math and strategic (chess) tasks. By forcing inter-agent agreement, it suppresses idiosyncratic per-instance errors and reduces 'confident hallucination' of facts the model is internally uncertain about. Relatedly exposes (but does not fully solve) the failure mode of superficial/overconfident self-reflection in single-agent settings.
dataset_or_benchmark_released: Yes — introduces a new Biographies factuality benchmark: ground-truth bullet-point biographies of 524 well-known computer scientists (facts extracted from Wikipedia), used to measure hallucination. Code and task scaffolding (arithmetic, GSM8K, biographies, MMLU) released at https://github.com/composable-models/llm_multiagent_debate.
builds_on: Society of Mind (Minsky 1988) as conceptual inspiration; AI safety via debate (Irving et al. 2018); single-model prompting techniques it complements/contrasts with — zero-shot chain-of-thought (Kojima et al. 2022), self-consistency / majority voting (Wang et al. 2022; Cobbe et al. 2021), scratchpads (Nye et al. 2021), and single-agent self-reflection (Reflexion, Shinn et al. 2023; Self-Refine, Madaan et al. 2023). Also builds on the authors' prior compositional/ensemble work (Li et al. 2022, composing ensembles of pre-trained models via iterative consensus).
extended_by_or_inspired: Spawned an extensive multi-agent debate / society-of-LLMs literature, e.g. 'More Agents Is All You Need' (Li et al. 2024, agent sampling-and-voting), 'Encouraging Divergent Thinking in LLMs through Multi-Agent Debate' (MAD, Liang et al. 2023), ChatEval (multi-agent debate for evaluation, Chan et al. 2023), 'Diversity of Thought Elicits Stronger Reasoning in Multi-Agent Debate' (Hegazy 2024), 'Should we be going MAD?' / debate critiques (Smit et al. 2024), and broad use in LLM-as-a-society / multi-agent system surveys (e.g. MAST failure-mode taxonomy work). Also referenced as a baseline in agentic reasoning and self-improvement / distillation studies.
citation_count: ~1723 (Semantic Scholar, fetched 2026-06; influentialCitationCount 224). One of the most-cited multi-agent LLM papers.
reasoning_model_native: No — the method was developed and evaluated on gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 (and chatGPT vs Bard), pre-dating o1/R1-style models with built-in reflection. It is an external scaffold that adds reflection on top of non-reasoning models; whether debate still helps strong reasoning-native models is an open question raised by later follow-up work (and some find diminishing returns), but not studied in this paper.
on_policy_distillation_link: Indirect / proposed-only. The paper explicitly suggests debate transcripts could be 'distilled back to self-improve the original base model,' i.e. using debate as a data-generation engine for a self-improvement loop — conceptually adjacent to on-policy distillation / self-distillation — but no distillation or weight update is performed in this work.
sample_efficiency: Default reported gains use 3 agents x 2 rounds (~6 LLM generations per query). Ablations show performance rises monotonically with more agents and more rounds on arithmetic, with rounds saturating around 4 (little gain beyond 4 rounds); summarization lets the method scale to 5+ agents. Evaluations were run on ~100-300 problems per task.
